_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 5 Mathematics unit lecture film, Rules and Patterns. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Chapters follow the lesson's own steps 8-13: a rule builds a sequence forwards (step 8, 5,9,13,17 and 3,7,11,15), the rule read backwards from the gaps and the 2,4,6 vs 2,4,8 trap (step 9), the triangle-and-circle two-unknowns puzzle (step 10), squares and cubes caught by their gaps of gaps (step 11), the matchstick-square pattern and its +3 rule (step 12), and decimal hops past zero on a number line (step 13). Every number said is the lesson's own: 5,9,13,17 and 3,7,11,15; 2,4,6 and 2,4,8; triangle+circle=10, triangle-circle=4, triangle=7, circle=3; squares' gap of gaps of 2, cubes' 12,18,24; matchstick squares 4,7,10 and pattern 10's 31; and 2,1.5,1,0.5,0,-0.5 and 1-3=-2. Note for the owner: BRIEF.md's earlier draft said this lesson's third part reopens as the next lesson's first part; that was corrected in the BRIEF itself (2026-09-25) as a regex artefact, and this film's checking agent independently confirmed the same thing by reading both lessons' WORK entries directly - the three parts here are self-contained. Revised 2026-09-25 against the lead's review: 5Nc.04 (square AND triangular numbers) was claimed but only half-delivered - hiddensquares draws squares/cubes, shapepatterns draws matchstick squares, and neither is a triangular number; the lesson's own Step 12 'Dot staircase' (count(n) = n(n+1)/2, 1/3/6/10/15) is the triangular pattern and this film does not draw it. The beat budget was already at the 36-beat cap (checked with --dry before deciding), so a new beat was not free, and squares-cubes-and-roots.json already claims 5Nc.04 with a full triangular-numbers chapter (rows growing by one, 1/3/6/10, the 6+10=16 square fact) - so 5Nc.04 is dropped here rather than added a second time; hiddensquares and shapepatterns now carry no code. seqrule's beat 5 used to leave the 6th term an unresolved '?' after saying the rule fires 5 times; it now resolves it in the lesson's own shortcut shape (start + (n-1)*step), read off the start-3 row already on screen: 3 + 5x4 = 23 (the lesson's own default row, start 5 + 5x4 = 25, is the same shortcut one beat earlier in the film's own numbers). hiddensquares beats 3-4 (squares, cubes) said 'a gap of 2' and 'their gaps are 12,18,24' as if those were the first-order gaps; both are second-order (gaps of the gaps, per beat 2's own 'look at the gaps of the gaps instead'), so both now say 'the gaps of their gaps'. Checked and NOT applied: the About list and self-check (G p36) claim the lesson teaches finding a recursion rule from non-consecutive terms; every SEQS and HIDDEN entry in rules-and-patterns.html gives four consecutive terms, and no step gives a gapped one - reported under problems, not fixed, because the lesson is not this film's file.
title: Rules and Patterns
subtitle: Grade 5 Mathematics
objectives: Use the relationship between repeated addition of a constant and multiplication to find any term of a linear sequence.
Recognise the use of objects, shapes or symbols to represent two unknown quantities in addition and subtraction calculations.
Count on and count back in steps of constant size, and extend beyond zero to include negative numbers.

beats.say: 3, 7, 11, 15. Can you see the rule that makes this sequence?

at.rule: the rule that makes this sequence

beats.say: A term-to-term rule links every term to the very next one, step by step.
A sequence is a list of numbers in order, one after another. Each number in it is a term.
Pick a start number and a rule to follow. Start at 5, and the rule is add 4.
Use the rule again and again: 5, 9, 13, 17.
Start at 3 instead, with the very same rule: 3, 7, 11, 15.
The rule fires 5 times to reach the 6th term. That's 3, plus 5 times 4 — 23.

scenes.heading: Find the rule from the gaps

beats.say: Now you are given the terms, and the rule is hidden from you. Look closely at the gap.
2, 4, 6: the gap is 2 every time, so the rule is add 2.
2, 4, 8 starts the same way, but the next gap is 4, not 2.
So the rule is not add 2 after all. It doubles each time.
Always check every gap, never just the first one.
In this puzzle, a shape can stand for a number that nobody has told you yet.

at.unknown: a number that nobody has told you yet

beats.say: Triangle plus circle equals 10, the first fact.
Triangle minus circle equals 4, the second fact.
Add the two facts together, and the circle cancels itself out completely.
That leaves two triangles equal 14, so one triangle is 7.
Put 7 back into a fact, and the circle is 3.
Sometimes the gaps between one term and the next are not all the same.
When that happens, look at the gaps of the gaps instead.
Square numbers: the gaps of their gaps settle on 2.

at.gaptwo: the gaps of their gaps settle on 2

beats.say: Cube numbers grow faster: the gaps of their gaps are 12, 18, 24.
Add 4 has gaps of gaps of 0, because they never change.
Matchstick squares grow in a pattern too. Count the sticks in each one.
Pattern 1 uses 4 sticks. Pattern 2 uses 7 sticks.
Pattern 3 needs 10 sticks. The gap is always 3.
One more square shares a side, so it costs only 3 new sticks.
So pattern 10 needs 31 sticks, with no building at all.
A step in a sequence can be smaller than 1, and it can go past zero.
Start at 2, and subtract 0.5 on every hop.
2, 1.5, 1, 0.5, 0, then minus 0.5: every hop the same size.
From 1, subtract 3, and you land on minus 2, not on 2.
A rule builds a sequence. Always check every gap first.
Two facts about two shapes are always exactly enough.
Squares and cubes hide inside the gaps of the gaps.
Shapes on paper and hops along a line follow the very same rule.

at.shapesnl: Shapes on paper and hops along a line
